article.text:
**Three models, each on the work it's good at. A frontier model cracks the hard part, an efficient model finishes the job, and a decision model picks the moment to hand over.**
[](https://github.com/nace-ai/intern/actions/workflows/ci.yml)
[](LICENSE)
[](https://nace.ai)
[](https://discord.com/invite/nace-ai)
[How it works](#how-it-works) · [Install](#install) · [Results](#results) · [Questions](#questions) · [Decision model](#what-the-decision-model-does) · [Capabilities](#capabilities) · [Models](#models) · [Editors](#use-it-from-your-editor)
One model on its own is either too weak for hard tasks or too expensive for the easy parts. Intern is an
open-source coding harness that runs every task on three:
- **Frontier model.** The smart, pricey one: Claude Opus 5.5, Fable, Sol, Hy4. It reads the code, works out what
has to be done and does the hard part.
- **Efficient model.** The fast, cheap one: Hy4 Flash, DeepSeek Flash, Sonnet, or a model on your own machine. It
carries on with the rest of the job.
- **Decision model.** A small model between the turns: Drex Max, Jev. It picks the moment to hand over, searches and
reranks code and files, decides what to keep when the context fills up, and nudges the work out of circles.
On Terminal-Bench 2.1 (87 tasks), Claude Opus 5.5 handing over to Hy4 Flash passes **92.4% at $0.127 a task**. Opus
5.5 on its own passes 91.1–93.7% at $0.280–0.393 in Pi, Hermes and OpenCode, and Hy4 Flash on its own 82.3–83.5%.
It isn't tied to one pair of models:
| Terminal-Bench 2.1 · 87 tasks | FrontierHarness v1.1 · open weights | 62 terminal tasks · one vendor |
|---|---|---|
| **Opus 5.5 → Hy4 Flash** | **DeepSeek V4.1 Flash → Qwen3.8 27B** | **GPT-6.1 Sol → GPT-6 Luna** |
| 92.4% at **$0.127** a task | 65.3% at **$0.092** a task | 44/62 at **$0.143** a task |
| Opus 5.5 alone: 91–94% at $0.28–0.39 | cheaper than all 22 harnesses on the board | Sol alone $0.233, Codex CLI $0.274 |
[All results](#results)
_Claude Opus 5.5 finds and fixes the bug, the decision model hands over, and Hy4 Flash finishes the job for a few
tenths of a cent. Scripted models on a real project; `tests/readme_screenshot.py` makes it again._
## How it works
1. **The frontier model starts every task.** It reads the code, runs what fails and lays down the main fix.
2. **The decision model watches each turn.** It reads a compact cut of the session, built by code rather than a
model, and answers one question: is the main solution in place, has a check run it, and is what's left only
local repair and finishing? Two turns in a row at 0.7 or more, from turn 8 on, and it hands over.
3. **The efficient model finishes.** It takes over in the same workspace and conversation, runs the tests, fixes
what they show and wraps up. A run hands over once and never back; your next message starts on the frontier
model again.
4. **The decision model keeps the work on track the whole way.** Every fourth turn it checks for circles and nudges.
It searches when your models ask, and it picks which reads to keep when the context fills up.
The work splits unevenly by design. On the Terminal-Bench 2.1 run, Hy4 Flash made about two-thirds of the model
calls and half the output, for 1% of the cost:
| | Claude Opus 5.5, frontier | Hy4 Flash, efficient |
|---|---|---|
| Model calls | 35% | 65% |
| Output tokens, thinking included | 52% | 48% |
| Cost | 99% | 1% |
The [architecture](docs/architecture.md) has the details and the measurements behind each step.
## Install
```bash
# Python 3.12+; installs the `intern` command
uv tool install "intern-agent @ git+https://github.com/nace-ai/intern"
intern
```
The first time, `intern` opens on a setup that takes about a minute:
1. **Connect a provider.** OpenRouter is the one we recommend: one key runs every model, and you can sign in with
your browser instead of pasting a key. Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini and 20 more work too, as does a model on your
machine (Ollama, LM Studio, llama.cpp, vLLM, Kapitsa).
2. **Pick your…

hn.title: Launch HN: Onlook (YC W25) – An open-source developer tool for designers
hn.text:
Hey HN, I'm Daniel, founder of Onlook (https://github.com/onlook-dev/onlook and onlook.com).
Onlook is a desktop app that puts a canvas on top of your real codebase, letting you design directly in code with the agent you already use. Over 25,000 designers and developers have supported the project, 100+ have contributed, and it's been the #1 trending repo in the world twice. We just rebuilt the entire product as an agentic design tool, and open-sourced it to the community.
Here’s a demo video: (https://youtu.be/BogcYWf4siM)
If you're an engineer, traditional engineering tools are largely built for convergence, whereas designers tend to explore and diverge on ideas. Onlook gives designers a familiar canvas while managing all of the dev processes that get between them and making mind-blowing designs in code. Designers can work on a multiple simultaneous worktrees that run on the real app locally, and every change lands as a PR you can review or throw away, so there aren’t mockups to rebuild.
We built Onlook because we believe there needs to be a developer tool that works the way designers do.
More and more, designers are expected to work in code. Designers think by seeing, drafting, arranging variations, using references, and remixing ideas. That’s why the canvas has been the signature feature of design tools because it genuinely is useful for how messy the creative process is. Most of the challenge of using engineering tools for design work is that the first half of starting a project often takes mental bandwidth in of itself (What branch am I on? What page was that last exploration on?) and the second half is constrained by configuring your coded design to present itself (prompting design tools on top of what you’ve built or making temporary navigation for that specific state).
Some of you may remember our earlier Show HNs (July 2024: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=40904862, August 2024: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=41390449, May 2025: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=44127653). Since then, we built a web version (too early), then a Storybook-native build (a mistake). We noticed that our desktop product from July 2024 was still getting hundreds of downloads a month despite zero promotion, so we decided to rebuild it for the new era of designers working in code.
How it works…
Onlook shines at exploring tons of ideas at once. Ask it to lay out every flow in your product, show every state of a component, or riff on ten versions of one screen. Your designs all show up side by side on an infinite canvas, with each frame as a real webview running your actual app with real data. Not as a mockup, but the real deal.
When we built this editor, we had an epiphany that it could be a new kind of IDE for design. Design tools used to be limited to a proprietary setup or closed schema, but now you can push and pull the medium of code to get whatever result you want, so why not give agents an infinite canvas of browsers and see what they do? It turns out, the agents can figure out how to better present coded work by adjusting the urls of browser frames and arranging and resizing them on the canvas.
The concept is simple, but it requires a lot of product thinking. For example, because all of the frames on the canvas share a single browser session, and Chromium only allows six connections per host per session, ten frames of the same app end up fighting over limited connections. So, we had to plan around that, and there are still tons of things we need to do to make the canvas ultra performant.
Onlook is an Electron app where you can import a repo from GitHub or upload a local folder. Then, Onlook creates a git worktree, starts your dev server, and has the agent sort out missing dependencies or other requirements. You never open a terminal and everything the agent does is a normal git diff that can go to GitHub as a PR. We inject a small script into each frame that draws selection outlines and reads the page, so that way you can…

# An Open-Source, Visual-First Canvas for Code
Craft websites, prototypes, and designs with AI on a canvas built for creative work. See
your real app running live, shape it visually, and let your own agent write the code. An
open-source alternative to Figma, V0, Replit Agent, Base 44, Webflow, etc.
## Why Onlook
- 🎨 **Built for design.** Onlook is the open-source developer tool for designers. You see your real app running live on a canvas, explore ideas side by side, and shape the interface visually instead of from a terminal. Design apps, websites, posters, graphics, and more with your local fonts and assets.
- 🤖 **Bring your own agent.** We don't ship our own model. Connect the Claude Code or ChatGPT/Codex account you already have, and that agent does the work inside your project. Plug in more tools through MCP connectors to bring all of the context you need to your creative workflow. Work on multiple design tasks at once across repos and pages.
- 📁 **Works on your real repo.** Onlook opens any Git repository on your machine and runs your own dev server, so what you design is your actual product, not a mockup that someone has to rebuild later.
- 🖥️ **A desktop app, local-first.** Onlook runs on your computer. Your code stays on your computer, and the source build needs no Onlook account, cloud keys, or `.env` file.
- 📤 **Share what you make.** Export artifacts as self-contained HTML, PNG, JPEG, or PDF to hand off, review, or post.
- 🧡 **Open source.** Apache 2.0. Read it, fork it, and customize it yourself (we'd love to hear how you customize it!)
## What you can do with Onlook
- [x] Design on your real codebase
- [x] Live app on an infinite canvas
- [x] Mobile, tablet, and desktop frames side by side
- [x] Safe worktree copy, so your folder is never touched
- [x] Parallel projects as tabs
- [x] Design with your own agent
- [x] Bring your own Claude Code or ChatGPT/Codex plan
- [x] Ask about any element on the canvas
- [x] Agent arranges the canvas for you (variations, states, flows)
- [x] Reference images on the canvas
- [x] Sketch and share
- [x] Artifacts for quick HTML sketches outside your repo
- [x] Export to HTML, PDF, PNG, and JPEG
- [x] Ship it
- [x] Import a GitHub repo
- [x] Start entirely new codebases from scratch
- [x] One-press pull requests, from checks to merge
## Getting Started
🖥️ [Download the Desktop App](https://www.onlook.com/install) (Recommended) – The fastest way to get started with Onlook.
* macOS (Apple Silicon · Intel x64) → [Download](https://www.onlook.com/install)
* Windows – Coming soon. Join the [Windows waitlist here](https://www.onlook.com/waitlist?os=windows) and be emailed when we have updates.
* Linux – No Linux artifact is published and we're still gauging demand for Linux. Join the [Linux waitlist here](https://www.onlook.com/waitlist?os=linux) and be emailed when we have updates.
🧑‍💻 Build from source – [SOURCE_BUILD.md](SOURCE_BUILD.md) covers building and running Onlook on a Mac. No Onlook account or cloud keys needed.

article.title: LLM assisted reverse engineering · Slow Chronicle
article.text:
LLM assisted reverse engineering
By ioma8
18 Nov 2026
Tags: reverse engineering, rust, ai, ghidra
I have been hacking both hardware and software for 2 decades. Previously manually. But in 2026 with the help of AIs the proccess is greatly sped up. Below I will describe my proccess briefly or how I do it.
Set Up
Tools which I mostly use are these:
TOOL
use
DeepSeek Harness + Deepseek v4.1 Flash
Thats the AI I am using. Occasionaly I use Codex with Luna or Terra but Deepseek is super performant, fast and cheap
Ghidra + MCP bridge
The best in the market, free, disassembler and decompiler. With the MCP bridge agents can use it very well
radare2 and kuna
CLI disassemblers and decompilers. Not as good as Ghidra but much faster and possibly better usable for AIs
Process
What I basically do nowadays is just point the agent at the binary to be analysed and use my set of dedicated agent skills. Rest usually takes care of itself. But putting the skills besides, the flow is basically this.
Find binary type, platform, build etc - based on this using appropriate decompiler (note - current AIs do fairly well with just disassembly . ie pure x86 or ARM instructions).
Command agent to document all findings along the way to MD files. This serves several purposes. They become notes for your own understanding. They help the agent not lose the track after compaction / handoff to different agent. And last but not least, it helps the agent work more effectively, not get lost in circles etc. More about this later.
Ask the agent to analyse basic structure. Main functions, main branching, imported functions etc of given binary. By binary I mean whatever. Desktop executable, website or firmware image.
Once I have this basic overview I can usually proceed any way I need to do modifications to the original binary or build mods or just help me understand it better.
On some occasions some things are not easily resolvable by simple disassembly or decompilation. In those cases you can do:
Let the agent debug given binary and set breakpoints on specific parts to help it figure out given inner workings.
Use logging. Either by somehow enabling it in the original binary or by making a probe (and this can mean many things) that injects to the original binary and records you via logs (to file) whatever is needed to resolve given feature.
Give agent outside access - ie computer use for desktop apps, or api controllable emulator for running and controlling given firmware.
Ask agent to try different approach. But you must be specific. Ie when it gets stuck in disasembly by following xrefs, ask it to try to follow strings in the binary instead.
Read the entire LLM conversation and thinking. Current LLMs are smart but they still sometimes get to a narrow approach. By reading the traces you can often instinctively figure the agent it going into a blind path and give it suggestion as to how it might be approached better. That however skill of your own to have.
SKILLS
Here are some of my major skills I use frequently.
Matt Pottock - Grill me
It gives you several questions when your input might be valuable. I usually use it with this prompt:
text
Use skill /grill-me to ask me up to 5 questions
whose answers are crucial for your further progress.
Ask only one question at a time.
mattpocock/skillsShellSkills for Real Engineers. Straight from my .agents directory.Open repo ↗Opens in a new tab.
Ghidra / other RE tooling skill
It helps a ton to have a skill where your specific reverse engineering tooling is described. Ie to use radare2 or kuna. Or description of how to use the MCP Ghidra bridge and for what. Without such a skill, agents often give up too quickly getting lost, not knowing how to do the actual disassembly / decompilation.
ioma8/ghidra-decompile-skillJavaAgent skill + 22 Ghidra scripts for fast targeted decompilation, and the fix for GhidraMCP extension/Ghidra version mismatches.Open repo ↗Opens in a new tab.
Hypothesis debugging
That is also my own skill. Its…

Introducing Volcano, a self-healing agent cloud by Kong
ProductBy Marco PalladinoNovember 19, 2026
Discuss on X
One place to build, host, and run agents and applications, with a platform that finds and fixes bugs on its own.
Building agents and applications in the AI era requires new primitives that we simply didn't need a few years ago. And even then, the pace of building has increased exponentially beyond what humans can do with traditional workflows. To make this worse, building agents became more of an exercise of composing together different services and platforms which compounds the complexity and maintenance requirements in the long run.
There must be a better way.
And this is why today we are announcing Volcano, a new self-healing agent cloud that provides in one place everything developers need to build agents and applications at scale. Volcano hosts all applications, agents, data storage and other capabilities that can be used seamlessly from your favorite coding harness (Cursor, Codex, Claude Code, and more) — or online via the easy-to-use builder experience — to go from idea to production in a fully automated way.
And then — once your agents, backends and frontends are running in Volcano — Volcano kicks in and works for you to continuously identify issues and provide resolutions to bugs so that your codebase gets better over time autonomously with no human intervention. By offering everything you need in one platform, you can also enormously simplify your implementations, which will be self-healing along the way.
We decided to build Volcano as a result of our experience at Kong building agents for ourselves, and what we learned from the 1000+ largest enterprise organizations that we work with. Kong processed more than a quadrillion requests for its customers in the last 12 months, and today we are finally enabling everyone to build in the AI era the way it's supposed to be.
Give it a try and let us know what you think, at volcano.dev.

article.title: I stopped knowing my own software · turri
article.text:
blog
I stopped knowing my own software
Why I built turri.
Žan Jonke·11 november 2026·15 min read
With great power…
I am a software engineer, so my job is engineering. Before AI, I did most of it by writing and reading code. I didn't know every line of the codebases that I worked on by heart, but I knew its shape, how it functions and how it behaves. I knew how it works.
Then I started using coding agents, and that knowledge began to slip away. Slowly, and with my full cooperation.
With an agent, a product comes together fast. Really fast. A feature an hour, sometimes more. Each one is a few thousand lines of code. I can't review thousands of lines every hour. Nobody can.
So I gave in. I stopped reviewing the code and started judging the software by its behaviour instead. It does the thing? Good, next feature. I started caring less and less about how things work and more and more about whether they work.
Addy Osmani has a name for where I ended up. In Critical thinking when agents do the work he describes a slide in three steps. First you offload: you delegate the task but keep ownership of the result. Then you defer: the tool's output becomes your next input. Finally you surrender: "the AI's output quietly becomes your own, you feel no need to check it." He credits the term cognitive surrender to Steven Shaw and Gideon Nave at Wharton.
I recognised every step. Each one felt reasonable at the time.
Ultimately I ended up accountable for software I did not understand. When it broke, it would be my name on it, and I could not say why it broke or whether a fix was right.
And software does break. Once real people use it, they find the paths nobody tested, and something gives. Understanding the software is what lets you find the cause at three in the morning. It is what lets you change one part without breaking another. It is what lets you tell a customer, or an auditor, what the system does with their data. Without it, every incident is a guess, every change is a gamble, and every answer starts with "I think".
Yes, a coding agent can do all of that too, often faster than I can. But how do I know it did the right thing? To check its answer, I have to understand the software myself.
The whole spirit of engineering is knowing how things work deeply enough to predict them, change them and explain them. I couldn't do any of that anymore.
This is why I created turri - to gain back control over engineering and let the coding agent handle the coding.
A chimp driving a car
I want to be fair first. Coding agents are remarkable. They write in minutes what took a team weeks. They get better with every model.
So this is not a post about agents being bad at coding. They are good at it and code got cheap. I am completely comfortable saying that a coding agent can write better code than I.
But what didn't change is the human using the coding agent. Give a chimp a car and you do not get a driver. You get a chimp, going very fast, about to crash.
A chimp driving a car.
A human with a coding agent is still a human. They read at the same speed they always did. They can hold as much in their head as they always could. Coding got faster. Human understanding did not.
What troubles me
I am not engineering anymore
Engineering, to me, is making decisions on purpose and being able to defend them. Those decisions start with understanding the problem at hand, doing the research and thinking it through. Only then comes designing a solution that is solid, scalable and durable. Even the word says so. Engineering comes from the Latin ingenium, meaning cleverness or a clever idea, the same root as ingenious. With an agent I was mostly typing wishes and accepting diffs. There was nothing ingenious about it.
And I tried what everyone recommends. I had the agent plan before it wrote any code, and I reviewed the plan. But then the plan was thrown away? Back to the code, I guess. I had it grill me with questions until it understood what I wanted. I explained the what,…

article.title: Snapchat now lets developers build AR Lenses with AI assistants like Claude Code and Cursor | TechCrunch
article.text:
Snapchat announced on Wednesday that it’s giving Lens creators the ability to build Lenses using the AI coding assistants they already use, like Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex. Snapchat Lenses, which are a core part of the social network’s platform, are AR effects that let users alter their appearance, add digital objects to their surroundings, or interact with animated experiences through the camera.
The company is introducing Easy Lens CLI, which builds on its existing Easy Lens tool, which lets creators generate Lenses from a single prompt on the web and mobile. Easy Lens CLI brings that same idea into developers’ existing workflows, allowing AI assistants to handle the technical work while creators focus on the vision for the Lens itself.
The launch indicates that Snapchat is looking to lower the barrier to creating AR content, while making its platform more accessible to developers who are increasingly using AI coding assistants. Instead of requiring creators to learn how to use Snapchat’s own development tools, the company is bringing Lens creation into the AI coding workflows they already use, which could in turn expand the pool of people who build for Snapchat.
Image Credits:Snapchat
Developers enrolled in Snapchat’s Lens+ Payouts program can earn from the Lenses they create with Easy Lens CLI. Snapchat says it paid out $1.8 million to Lens+ community creators last month.
Lens creators can describe the Lens they want in plain language, and their AI assistant handles the process from start to finish, Snapchat says. That includes building with more than 100 AR building blocks and 50 AI asset generators, generating previews, and publishing them to Snapchat and tracking their performance.
With Easy Lens CLI, Snapchat says developers can create everything from Web Lens games with leaderboards to camera effects and beauty filters.
AI assistants can generate assets, build and test Lenses, address errors, and send updated versions directly to the creator’s phone. The new capability can take a game from an initial idea to a published Lens in a single day, without developers having to write code themselves, Snapchat says.
The tool is aimed at different types of creators. The company notes that game developers can bring existing browser games to Snapchat as Web Lenses, while AI creators can use assets from their preferred tools to build Lenses in their own style. Additionally, agencies and brands can turn existing campaign videos, images, and other brand assets into AR experiences with less production time.
Easy Lens CLI runs on Mac, Windows, and Linux.
